title: Tools described as schemas
objectives: Write tool definitions as JSON schemas and validate arguments against them.

screens.title: The model reads only the label
screens.prose: There is no language model in this course's browser, so the agents here run against a **scripted model**: fixed replies, the same every run, built to show real behaviours. It picks by description, as a real model leans on it (a real one also reads names and schemas). Below, three tools are offered under the uninformative names tool_a, tool_b and tool_c, with the same vague description, 'Gets data.', for the question about CORR's close.

params.title: Vague descriptions
lines: user: [D01] What was CORR's close on 2024-03-08?
model: call tool_a {"query": "What was CORR's close on 2024-03-08?"}

screens.question: Which tool did the scripted model call?

options.text: tool_b, which is the price tool underneath
options.why: That is the right tool, but nothing in 'Gets data.' or its name told the model so.
It took the first tool on the list, tool_a.
It called a tool; the trace shows tool_a.

hints.text: Read the second line of the trace.

feedback.correct: tool_a, which is search_notes underneath: with nothing to choose by, it took the first tool, and answered 'note 101' to a price question.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the model's call in the trace.

explain.text: A model sees each tool's name, description and argument schema. With nothing to tell three tools apart, it guessed, confidently and wrongly.

screens.title: Fix the description
screens.prose: Now the tools carry their real names and descriptions; get_close's says 'Closing price of one share on one trading day.' Tap the line where the model's choice changes.

params.title: Clear descriptions
lines: user: [D01] What was CORR's close on 2024-03-08?

screens.question: Tap the model's tool call.

hints.text: The model's call is the line after the user's question.

feedback.correct: It called get_close with the ticker and date, and answered 97.87, the right close.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Tap the line that starts 'model: call'.

byKey.l4: That is the answer; the choice was made at the call above it.

explain.text: The same scripted model, the same question: only the descriptions changed. **The description is the interface**: it is all the model knows about what a tool does.

screens.title: A schema for get_close
screens.prose: Each tool also gets a **JSON schema** for its arguments: their types, which are `required`, allowed values (`enum`), number bounds, and whether other keys are refused. The harness checks every call against it before running the tool.

rows: one of CORR, DUNM, ELRY, HALL; required

screens.question: Which arguments pass get_close's schema?

options.why: The date must be a string; 20240308 is an integer.
'Corran' is not in the ticker enum.
Extra keys are refused: 'adj' is not a field.

hints.text: Check type, enum and extra keys for each.

feedback.correct: Only the first: right types, a ticker from the enum, no extra keys.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each field against the table.

explain.text: A schema turns rules into checks a program can run, so a bad call is caught before it reaches the price table.

screens.title: Count the errors
screens.prose: A call arrives with `{"ticker": "Apple Inc.", "k": 5}` for get_close.

rows: one of CORR, DUNM, ELRY, HALL; required

screens.question: How many separate errors does the schema report?

hints.text: Check the required fields, then each key given.
date is missing; ticker is not in the enum; k is not a field.

feedback.correct: Three: missing 'date', 'ticker' not one of the four, and unexpected 'k'.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check required, enum and extra keys.

byKey.one: More than one rule is broken: also check the enum and the extra key.
byKey.two: You missed one: the missing date, the ticker outside the enum, and the extra 'k'.

explain.text: All 3 errors, reported at once, let the model fix them in one turn instead of three.

screens.title: Number bounds
screens.prose: search_notes takes `query` (a string) and `k` (an integer from 1 to 10). A model asks for `{"query": "corran debt", "k": 50}`.
screens.question: What should the harness do?

options.text: Refuse the call: k must be at most 10

options.why: Silently changing a call hides the mistake; the model never learns the limit.
The schema's maximum is there to stop exactly this.

options.text: Drop k and use the default
options.why: That is another silent change.

feedback.correct: Refuse it, saying why, and let the model ask again.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What is the schema for?

explain.text: The bound is enforced by code, not hoped for. The refusal goes back to the model as a tool result it can act on.

screens.title: Saying it instead of checking it
screens.prose: A colleague's get_close schema has `ticker: {"type": "string"}` and a description that says 'use the exchange ticker, e.g. CORR'. A model sends `"ticker": "Corran Group"`.

rows: one of CORR, DUNM, ELRY, HALL; required

screens.question: What happens?

options.text: The call passes the schema and reaches the price table, which has no 'Corran Group'

options.why: A description is text the model may ignore; nothing in the code checks it.

options.text: The model never sends names, since the description says not to
options.why: Models often follow descriptions, not always; the rule must be checked.

options.text: It works: the table looks names up
options.why: The table is keyed by ticker only.

hints.text: Which of the two, schema or description, is checked by code?

feedback.correct: Any string passes, so the bad ticker reaches the table and fails there, or worse, matches something wrong.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does the schema actually check?

byKey.blocked: You trusted the description to enforce a rule. Only the schema is checked: add an `enum` of tickers.

explain.text: Rules the code must enforce belong in the schema (`enum: ["CORR", "DUNM", "ELRY", "HALL"]`); the description helps the model, it does not police it.

screens.title: A tool with no arguments
screens.prose: A tool `market_status()` takes no arguments: its schema is `{"type": "object", "properties": {}, "additionalProperties": false}`.
screens.question: Which arguments pass?

options.why: 'when' is an extra key, refused; and an empty string is not an object.

options.text: None: a tool must have arguments
options.why: An empty object is valid arguments.
Arguments must be an object; a string is not.

hints.text: Arguments are always an object, even an empty one.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the type and the extra key.

explain.text: A tool with no arguments still gets an object, `{}`; anything inside it is an extra key.

screens.title: A tool is a contract
screens.prose:
What you built: a tool is a name, a description the model reads, and a schema the harness checks,

```text
{"name": "get_close",
 "description": "Closing price of one share...",
 "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {...},
                  "required": [...], "additionalProperties": false}}
```

This is the shape Anthropic's API uses; others rename `input_schema`.
screens.question: Where does a rule such as 'k is at most 10' belong?

options.text: In the schema, where code checks it
In the description, where the model reads it
options.why: Say it there too if it helps, but only the schema is checked.

options.text: Inside the tool, as a crash
options.why: A crash inside the tool is a worse message than a schema error.
Prompts guide; they do not enforce.

hints.text: Which part is checked by code?

feedback.correct: In the schema; the description may repeat it for the model's sake.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which part is enforced?

explain.text: Descriptions steer, schemas enforce. Write both: the description for the model, the schema for the harness.

screens.title: validate in code
screens.prose: Write `validate(args, schema)` for the parts of JSON schema used here: object arguments, `required`, `properties` with a `type` of string, integer, number or boolean, `enum`, `minimum`, `maximum` and `additionalProperties`. No `jsonschema` package: a small validator is enough. `TYPE_NAMES` maps a Python type to its schema name.
screens.question: Write `validate`.

widget.starter:
def validate(args, schema):
    # list of error strings, any order:
    #   "missing required field 'x'"
    #   "unexpected field 'x'"          (when additionalProperties is false)
    #   "field 'x' must be T, got U"    (T a schema type, U from TYPE_NAMES)
    #   "field 'x' must be one of a, b, c"
    #   "field 'x' must be at least m" / "... at most m"
    # a type error ends the checks for that field; non-dict args give
    # ['arguments must be an object']
    ...
widget.prelude:
import numpy
TYPE_NAMES = {str: 'string', bool: 'boolean', int: 'integer', float: 'number', list: 'array', dict: 'object', type(None): 'null'}

widget.how: Submit runs 11 hidden tests, each an exact sorted list. They cover a good call, a missing field, an integer date, a name outside the enum with an extra key, a boolean and a decimal where an integer is wanted, and k above and below its bounds. The rest are a number where an enum string is wanted, arguments that are not an object, and an empty schema.

mutants.symptom: Keeps checking a field after its type error.
Checks the maximum but not the minimum.
Accepts 2.5 where an integer is wanted.

hints.text: Check required names first, then loop over the given keys.
In Python `isinstance(True, int)` is True: rule booleans out of integer and number.

feedback.correct: Your validator matches on every test.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: A call with no date must report "missing required field 'date'".
byKey.test-8: After a type error, skip the field's other checks: a number for the ticker is one error, not two.
byKey.test-4: 'k' is not a get_close field: report "unexpected field 'k'".
byKey.test-5: In Python True is an int; refuse booleans where an integer is wanted.
byKey.test-7: k = 0 is below the minimum of 1: report it.
byKey.test-11: 2.5 is a number but not an integer: refuse it where an integer is wanted, and say it got a number.

explain.text: Returning every error as a sentence, not raising on the first, gives the model one message it can fix everything from.

screens.title: tool_spec in code
screens.prose: Write `tool_spec(fn, description, schema)`, building the record a model is shown. Refuse a blank description, since it is the model's only guide, and a schema that is not an object.
screens.question: Write `tool_spec`.

tests.setup: from llm_apps_ops_l3 import get_close, SCHEMAS, DESCRIPTIONS

widget.how: Submit runs 5 hidden tests: the name and the keys of get_close's spec, the name taken from a built-in function, and ValueError for a blank description and for a schema that is not an object.

feedback.correct: Your spec matches the shape on every test.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Use the keys name, description and input_schema.
byKey.test-4: A description of spaces tells the model nothing: refuse it after stripping.
byKey.test-3: Take the name from the function: `fn.__name__`.

explain.text: Refusing a blank description at build time is cheaper than discovering, in a trace, that the model guessed.

screens.title: An internal data API
screens.prose: A research team wraps its internal fundamentals API as a tool for an assistant. The API takes a company id (an integer from the security master) and a field name from a list of 40.
screens.question: Which schema choice prevents the most bad calls?

options.text: Make `field` an enum of the 40 names, `company_id` an integer, both required
Describe the 40 fields in the description and accept any string
options.why: The model may still send a near-miss name; only an enum stops it.

options.text: Accept any arguments and let the API return its errors
options.why: The API's errors may be cryptic; the schema's are written for the model.

options.text: Make company_id a string so names also work
options.why: Then 'Corran' reaches an API keyed by integers.

hints.text: Which rules can a schema check?

feedback.correct: An enum and types catch bad calls before they reach the API, with messages the model can act on.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which option puts the rules in the schema?

explain.text: Put every checkable rule in the schema. The description then explains meaning (what each field is), not validity.

ideas: A tool is a name, a description and a JSON schema; the model sees only these, so the description is the interface.
The harness validates every call against the schema (types, required, enum, bounds, no extra keys) before running anything.
Rules that matter go in the schema, where code checks them; a description guides the model but enforces nothing.

formula.note: The shape Anthropic's API uses; others rename `input_schema`.

summary.trap: A ticker typed as any string, with the rule only in the description: 'Corran Group' reaches the price table.

quiz.prose: get_close's schema requires ticker and date and refuses extra keys. A call sends `{"date": "2024-03-08", "adj": true}`.
quiz.question: How many errors should `validate` report?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check required and extra keys.

byKey.one: Both the missing ticker and the extra key count.

explain.text: The missing required field and the extra key are separate errors: 2.

quiz.prose: A schema says `k` is an integer. In Python, `isinstance(True, int)` is `True`.
quiz.question: Should `{"k": true}` pass?

options.text: Yes: True is an int in Python, so it counts
options.why: JSON's true is a boolean; treating it as 1 hides a mistake.
Silently reading true as 1 hides the model's error.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Is a JSON boolean an integer?

explain.text: `bool` is a subclass of `int` in Python, so test `isinstance(value, bool)` before accepting an integer.

quiz.prose: Two tools have the same description, 'Gets data.', and uninformative names.
quiz.question: What does a model use to choose between them?

options.text: Little more than their order: it is guessing

options.why: The model never sees the code.

options.text: Only their schemas, which are enough
options.why: Schemas show arguments, which help, but here nothing else tells the tools apart.
It sees results only after calling.

feedback.generic: Not quite. What does the model see?

explain.text: The model sees name, description and schema. With equal descriptions and names it has little to go on.
